## Goal

By hand and in R, calculate analyte amount from standardised titrant, explain
why an observed endpoint only estimates equivalence, and report an EDTA result
on an explicit CaCO₃ equivalent basis. Use a pH curve to reason about endpoint
choice rather than memorising “stop at pH 7”.

## Background

For the strong-acid reaction $\mathrm{H^++OH^-\rightarrow H_2O}$, equivalence
means equal reacted amounts. With 1:1 stoichiometry,
$c_a=c_bV_{eq}/V_a$. Read delivered burette volume as final minus initial, then
subtract justified blank consumption on the same volume basis. A measured
endpoint estimates $V_{eq}$ under a stated indicator or numerical rule.

At 25 °C the ideal strong-acid/strong-base equivalence has pH 7. A weak acid's
conjugate base changes equivalence pH without changing the number of moles that
must be neutralised. The supplied weak-acid comparison uses pKa 4.76.

For this simplified hardness procedure assume accessible Ca and Mg react
selectively 1:1 with EDTA under the supplied conditions. Report the combined
amount as CaCO₃ using 100.09 g/mol. This equivalent basis does not prove that
carbonate was present or distinguish Ca from Mg. All course data are simulated.

## By hand

**B1.** A 25.00 mL strong-acid aliquot reaches its estimated endpoint after
25.00 mL of standardised 0.1000 mol/L base. Calculate acid concentration and
reacted amount. Show where litres are necessary. [Hint](#hint-b1)

**B2.** The same initial amount is instead a weak monoprotic acid. Does its
equivalence require less base? Must equivalence still occur at pH 7? Explain
using stoichiometry and equilibrium separately. [Hint](#hint-b2)

**B3.** A 50.00 mL water sample uses EDTA at 0.01000 mol/L. Burette readings
are 0.10 and 6.30 mL; a matched blank consumes 0.05 mL. Calculate metal amount
and hardness as mg/L CaCO₃. Predict the error direction if the blank is omitted.
[Hint](#hint-b3)

**B4.** An electrode reads pH 6.0 at 24.90 mL and 8.0 at 25.10 mL. Calculate
the finite-difference pH slope and its assigned midpoint volume. Explain why
using only the row difference is wrong if addition volumes vary. [Hint](#hint-b4)

## In R

Open the supplied project at its root. The following workflow runs in a fresh
R session and does not require a demo export. It uses your earlier `read_csv`,
`mutate` and plotting skills, adding `diff()` for consecutive changes.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
curve <- read_csv("data/course/acid-titration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
slopes <- data.frame(
  midpoint_ml = (head(curve$volume_ml, -1) + tail(curve$volume_ml, -1)) / 2,
  ph_per_ml = diff(curve$ph) / diff(curve$volume_ml))
ggplot(curve, aes(volume_ml, ph)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "0.1000 mol/L base added (mL)", y = "pH") + theme_minimal()
ggplot(slopes, aes(midpoint_ml, ph_per_ml)) + geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Addition midpoint (mL)", y = "Finite-difference pH per mL") +
  theme_minimal()
acid_mol_l <- 0.1000 * 25.00 / 25.00
hardness <- read_csv("data/course/edta.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(delivered_ml = final_burette_ml - initial_burette_ml,
         corrected_ml = delivered_ml - blank_ml,
         moles_metal = edta_mol_l * corrected_ml / 1000,
         hardness_mg_l_CaCO3 = moles_metal * 100.09 * 1000 / (sample_ml / 1000))
hardness
write_csv(hardness, "output/titration-exercise.csv")
```

**R1.** Explain the units in each calculated column. Locate the steep region
and explain why the slope maximum is an exploratory check rather than complete
endpoint validation. [Hint](#hint-r1)

**R2.** Compare H1a, H1b and H2a. Which are independent preparations of the
same supplied sample, and which values may be described as separate waters?
State one source of uncertainty not estimated by their difference.
[Hint](#hint-r2)

**R3.** Independently calculate a new result for 25.00 mL water: 4.10 mL delivered
EDTA, 0.10 mL blank, 0.01000 mol/L titrant. Add the result and its correct unit
to your report. [Hint](#hint-r3)

## Hints

::: {#hint-b1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B1: amount before concentration"}
Use $n=cV$ with volume in litres, then divide by the original acid volume.
Matching millilitre units may cancel only when you use a volume ratio.
:::

::: {#hint-b2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B2: two different questions"}
Stoichiometry determines the amount of titrant; equilibrium determines species
and pH. A conjugate base remains after neutralising a weak acid.
:::

::: {#hint-b3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B3: delivered volume and reporting basis"}
First subtract initial from final, then the matched blank. EDTA mol equals
accessible metal mol in this scenario. Convert to equivalent CaCO₃ mass and
divide by the original sample volume.
:::

::: {#hint-b4 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="B4: use actual spacing"}
Divide 2.0 pH units by the difference in millilitres. The midpoint is the mean
of the two added volumes.
:::

::: {#hint-e1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E1: compare volume and pH separately"}
Read both equivalence outputs before inspecting the chosen endpoint. The initial
acid amount is held fixed by the model.
:::

::: {#hint-e2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E2: dilute titrant, fixed moles"}
Halving titrant concentration requires twice its volume for the same moles.
:::

::: {#hint-e3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="E3: endpoint bias is not reading precision"}
Compare the amount inferred at the trigger with the known model amount. The
simulation excludes noise, incomplete mixing and instrument/junction effects.
:::

::: {#hint-r1 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R1: read diff"}
[`diff`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/diff.html) gives consecutive differences.
Unequal volume steps require their own denominators; differentiation amplifies noise.
:::

::: {#hint-r2 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R2: inspect sample_id"}
Preparation IDs are not the same as independent collection IDs. Titrant
standardisation or endpoint bias can be common to several preparations.
:::

::: {#hint-r3 .callout-tip collapse="true" title="R3: reuse the model with a new denominator"}
The corrected volume is 4.00 mL, but this aliquot is 25.00 mL rather than 50.00 mL.
:::

## Solutions

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Full worked solutions"}
**B1.** Base amount is $0.1000\times0.02500=0.002500$ mol. The 1:1 reaction
therefore consumed 0.002500 mol acid. Dividing by 0.02500 L acid gives
**0.1000 mol/L**. Multiplying concentration by 25.00 without converting mL to L
would be a thousand-fold amount error.

**B2.** With the same monoprotic acid amount, the same base moles are required,
so equivalence volume remains 25.00 mL at the same base concentration. A weak
acid leaves its conjugate base at equivalence, and its pH can exceed 7. Acid
strength changes the pH curve, not the supplied number of acid moles.

**B3.** Delivered volume $6.30-0.10=6.20$ mL; corrected volume $6.20-0.05=6.15$
mL. Metal amount is $0.01000\times0.00615=6.15\times10^{-5}$ mol. Equivalent
CaCO₃ mass is $6.15\times10^{-5}\times100.09\times1000=6.155535$ mg. Divide by
0.05000 L to obtain **123.1107 mg/L as CaCO₃**. Omitting positive blank
consumption biases this estimate high. It is not a separate calcium result.

**B4.** $(8.0-6.0)/(25.10-24.90)=10.0$ pH units per mL, assigned to 25.00 mL.
The denominator represents actual added volume. A difference per row silently
assumes equal step sizes and can distort the inferred steep region.

**E1.** Equivalence volume stays fixed while weak-acid equivalence pH rises.
The pH 7 trigger is reached before weak-acid equivalence and underestimates the
acid amount in this model. No general rule sets every endpoint to pH 7.

**E2.** Required base moles remain 2.500 mmol. At 0.0500 mol/L, equivalence
volume is $0.002500/0.0500=0.05000$ L = **50.00 mL** for either acid model.
The changed base concentration, not acid strength, caused the volume change.

**E3.** A trigger below equivalence pH usually stops early and gives low inferred
acid; one above it stops late and gives high inferred acid. The precise volume
depends on pKa and trigger. This is a systematic endpoint-rule problem, not a
lack of printed precision. If the selected trigger is already outside the
displayed titration range, it is unavailable rather than evidence of zero
acid. The ideal model does not supply real electrode,
volume, mixing or recovery uncertainty.

**R1.** Delivered/corrected volumes are mL, metal amount mol, hardness mg/L as
CaCO₃. The slope plot locates a steep region near 25 mL; its value depends on
step sizes and noise. A validated endpoint method must address these effects.

**R2.** H1a/H1b are separate preparations of H1, giving **123.1107** and
**124.1116 mg/L as CaCO₃**. H2a is another supplied sample at **191.1719 mg/L**.
Two preparations of one water do not become two independently collected waters.
Shared titrant concentration uncertainty or endpoint bias is not established
from their difference.

**R3.** The corrected consumption is 0.00400 L; amount is $4.00\times10^{-5}$
mol, equivalent to 4.0036 mg CaCO₃ in 0.02500 L. Result is **160.144 mg/L as
CaCO₃**:

```r
new_hardness <- 0.01000 * ((4.10 - 0.10) / 1000) *
                  100.09 * 1000 / (25.00 / 1000)
new_hardness
```
:::
